title: Calories in Alcohol: Beer, Wine, Liquor and Cocktails Chart
excerpt: How many calories are in alcohol? A chart for beer, wine, shots, and cocktails, the simple 7-calories-per-gram math for any drink, and what alcohol calories do in your body.
metaDescription: Calories in alcohol: a chart for beer, wine, liquor, and cocktails, the 7-calories-per-gram math for any drink, and how alcohol affects weight.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The short answer:** pure alcohol has about **7 calories per gram**, almost twice as much as sugar or protein (4 calories per gram) and not far behind fat (9 calories per gram). One US standard drink holds 14 grams of alcohol, so every standard drink carries roughly **100 calories from the alcohol alone**, before you count any sugar, carbs, or mixers. A regular beer lands around 150 calories, a 5-ounce glass of wine around 120 to 125, and a shot of 80-proof liquor around 100. Cocktails are where the numbers jump, because syrups, juices, and cream can easily double or triple the total.

This guide gives you the chart, the simple math to work out any drink yourself, and an honest look at what those calories actually do in your body, including why a night out tends to cost more calories than the drinks themselves.

> **A note on the numbers.** Calorie figures for alcoholic drinks vary by brand, recipe, pour size, and alcohol strength. The values below are typical approximations based on standard serving sizes and published nutrition data. Check a brand's own nutrition panel when one is available. If you are managing diabetes, a medical condition, or a medication that interacts with alcohol, talk to your doctor about what's right for you.

## Why Alcohol Has Calories: The 7 Calories per Gram Rule

Calories are just a measure of how much energy your body can get from something. The three main nutrients your body runs on are carbohydrates, protein, and fat. Alcohol (ethanol) is a fourth source of energy, even though it isn't a nutrient you need.

| Energy source | Calories per gram |
|---|---|
| Carbohydrate | 4 |
| Protein | 4 |
| **Alcohol (ethanol)** | **7** |
| Fat | 9 |

That 7 calories per gram figure is the standard value used in nutrition labeling and dietetics. It means alcohol is an unusually dense source of energy. A drink with no sugar at all, like vodka and soda water, still carries real calories because the alcohol itself is the fuel.

People often call alcohol calories "empty calories." That doesn't mean they don't count. It means they come with essentially no vitamins, minerals, fiber, or protein. Your body gets the energy and very little else.

## The Calories in Alcohol Chart

Here are typical calorie counts for common drinks at standard US serving sizes. Treat these as reasonable estimates, not exact values. A heavy pour, a stronger craft beer, or a sweeter recipe will push the number up.

### Beer

| Drink | Typical serving | Approx. calories |
|---|---|---|
| Light beer (around 4% ABV) | 12 oz | 95 to 110 |
| Regular lager (around 5% ABV) | 12 oz | 140 to 155 |
| IPA (6 to 7% ABV) | 12 oz | 180 to 240 |
| Double IPA or imperial stout (8 to 10%+ ABV) | 12 oz | 250 to 350+ |
| Non-alcoholic beer (0.5% ABV or less) | 12 oz | 50 to 90 |
| Pint of regular beer (5% ABV) | 16 oz | around 200 |

### Wine

| Drink | Typical serving | Approx. calories |
|---|---|---|
| Dry white wine (around 12% ABV) | 5 oz | 115 to 125 |
| Dry red wine (around 13 to 14% ABV) | 5 oz | 120 to 130 |
| Rosé | 5 oz | 115 to 125 |
| Champagne or brut sparkling wine | 5 oz | 100 to 120 |
| Sweet dessert wine | 3 oz | 140 to 170 |
| Large restaurant pour | 8 to 9 oz | 190 to 230 |

### Spirits (straight, per 1.5 oz shot)

| Drink | Proof | Approx. calories |
|---|---|---|
| Vodka, gin, rum, tequila, whiskey | 80 proof (40%) | about 97 |
| Same spirits | 90 proof (45%) | about 110 |
| Same spirits | 100 proof (50%) | about 124 |
| Flavored or cream liqueurs | varies | 100 to 175+ |

Unflavored spirits have almost no carbs, so nearly all their calories come from the alcohol. That's why vodka, gin, tequila, and whiskey of the same proof land on almost the same number.

### Hard seltzers and cocktails

| Drink | Typical serving | Approx. calories |
|---|---|---|
| Hard seltzer (5% ABV) | 12 oz | about 100 |
| Vodka soda or gin and diet tonic | 1.5 oz spirit | about 100 |
| Gin and regular tonic | 1.5 oz gin + 4 oz tonic | 140 to 160 |
| Rum and cola | 1.5 oz rum + 6 oz cola | 160 to 190 |
| Hard cider | 12 oz | 160 to 220 |
| Margarita (restaurant) | 8 oz | 250 to 400+ |
| Long Island iced tea | 8 oz | 250 to 400+ |
| Piña colada | 8 to 10 oz | 350 to 550 |
| White Russian or mudslide | 6 to 8 oz | 300 to 500+ |

The spread on cocktails is wide on purpose. Bars use very different amounts of syrup, juice, and cream. A frozen margarita from a chain restaurant can carry several times the calories of one made with fresh lime juice and a small amount of agave.

## How to Calculate the Calories in Any Drink

You don't need a chart if you know two things: how much liquid is in the glass and how strong it is (the ABV, or alcohol by volume, printed on the label). The math takes about thirty seconds.

**Step 1: Work out the grams of alcohol.**

Multiply the serving size in milliliters by the ABV, then by 0.789 (the density of alcohol, meaning one milliliter of pure alcohol weighs about 0.79 grams).

- One US fluid ounce is about 29.6 mL.
- A 12-ounce beer is about 355 mL.

**Step 2: Multiply the grams of alcohol by 7.**

That gives you the calories from the alcohol itself.

**Step 3: Add the calories from carbs, if any.**

Carbs add 4 calories per gram. Beer, cider, wine, and mixers all contain some. Straight unflavored spirits contain essentially none.

### Worked example: a 12-ounce, 5% beer

- 355 mL × 0.05 = 17.75 mL of pure alcohol
- 17.75 × 0.789 = about 14 grams of alcohol
- 14 × 7 = about **98 calories from alcohol**
- A typical lager has around 12 to 13 grams of carbs, adding about 50 calories
- Total: roughly **150 calories**

### Worked example: an IPA at 7%

- 355 mL × 0.07 × 0.789 = about 19.6 grams of alcohol
- 19.6 × 7 = about **137 calories from alcohol**
- Add 15 to 20 grams of carbs (60 to 80 calories)
- Total: roughly **200 to 215 calories**

This is the most useful takeaway in the whole article: **strength matters more than style.** A 9% hazy IPA can carry more than twice the calories of a 4% light beer in the same size can, and most of the difference is the alcohol, not the carbs.

### A quick shortcut

If you don't want to do the math, use this rule of thumb: **every standard drink is about 100 calories of alcohol.** A US standard drink is 14 grams of alcohol, which equals 12 ounces of 5% beer, 5 ounces of 12% wine, or 1.5 ounces of 80-proof liquor. Then add whatever sugar or carbs the drink brings on top. In the UK, where a unit is 8 grams of alcohol, each unit is roughly 56 calories of alcohol.

## Calories in Beer

Beer gets its calories from two places: the alcohol and the leftover carbohydrates from the grain that weren't turned into alcohol during brewing.

- **Light beers** cut calories mainly by brewing to a lower alcohol level and fermenting out more of the sugars. That's how they get down to around 100 calories.
- **Regular lagers** at about 5% sit near 150 calories.
- **Craft beers** are where calories climb. Many IPAs, stouts, and Belgian styles are 6 to 10% alcohol or stronger, and some sweet or "pastry" styles leave in a lot of residual sugar too.
- **Pints and tall cans** quietly add up. A 16-ounce pint holds a third more than a 12-ounce bottle, and a 19.2-ounce can holds 60% more.

Breweries in the US aren't required to print calories on the can, though many larger brands publish them on their website or in a voluntary "Serving Facts" panel. If the label shows only ABV, the calculation above gets you close.

## Calories in Wine

Wine is fairly predictable. Most of its calories come from the alcohol, with a smaller contribution from any sugar left over after fermentation.

- **Dry wines** (most reds, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Grigio, brut sparkling) usually have very little sugar left, so a 5-ounce glass is mostly about the alcohol, landing around 115 to 130 calories.
- **Higher-alcohol wines** such as some Zinfandels, Syrahs, and Australian or Californian reds at 14.5 to 15% sit a bit higher.
- **Off-dry and sweet wines** (some Rieslings, Moscato, dessert wines, port) add sugar calories, which is why dessert wines are served in smaller glasses.

The biggest variable with wine is the pour. A standard serving is 5 ounces, but home pours and restaurant glasses are often 6 to 9 ounces. A bottle of wine (750 mL, about 25 ounces) at 13% alcohol contains roughly 600 to 650 calories, so splitting a bottle between two people is about 300 calories each.

## Calories in Liquor and Shots

Straight spirits are the simplest case. Unflavored vodka, gin, rum, tequila, and whiskey contain essentially no carbs, so their calories depend almost entirely on proof.

- **80 proof (40%):** about 97 calories per 1.5-ounce shot
- **86 proof (43%):** about 105
- **100 proof (50%):** about 124

Tequila is not lower in calories than vodka, and whiskey is not higher than gin, at the same proof. Claims that one clear spirit is "the low-calorie one" usually come down to marketing, not chemistry.

Liqueurs are a different story. Products like coffee liqueur, amaretto, triple sec, and cream liqueurs contain a lot of added sugar, and a 1.5-ounce pour can run 150 calories or more even though many of them are lower in alcohol than straight spirits.

A shot glass also isn't always 1.5 ounces. Some are 1 ounce and some "double" or novelty glasses hold 2 to 3 ounces, so count by what's actually in the glass.

## Calories in Cocktails and Mixed Drinks

With mixed drinks, the spirit is often the smaller share of the calories. The mixers do the heavy lifting.

Common mixers, per typical amount used:

- **Soda water, diet soda, diet tonic:** close to zero
- **Regular tonic water:** around 40 to 50 calories per 4 ounces (tonic is sweetened, which surprises many people)
- **Regular cola or ginger ale:** around 60 to 80 calories per 6 ounces
- **Orange or cranberry juice cocktail:** around 60 to 90 calories per 4 to 6 ounces
- **Simple syrup:** around 50 calories per half-ounce
- **Pre-made sour mix or margarita mix:** often 100 or more calories per serving
- **Cream, coconut cream, or ice cream:** can add 150 to 300+ calories on its own

So a gin and diet tonic is about 100 calories, while a piña colada made with coconut cream and pineapple juice can top 400. Frozen and blended drinks are typically the highest, because they're large, sweet, and easy to drink quickly.

### Lower-calorie swaps that still taste like a real drink

- Swap regular tonic or soda for the diet or zero-sugar version.
- Ask for fresh citrus instead of sour mix.
- Choose a highball (spirit plus a long mixer over ice) over a blended drink.
- Order a smaller size, or a "skinny" version made with less syrup.
- Make a spritz: wine topped with soda water stretches one glass into a longer drink.

For a full ranked list of the lightest options, see our guide to [the lowest-calorie alcohol](/never-hungover/lowest-calorie-alcohol).

## Does Your Body Treat Alcohol Calories Differently?

Yes, in a few important ways. This is where the "a calorie is a calorie" idea gets more interesting.

### Your body burns alcohol first

Your body has no good way to store alcohol, and it treats it as something to clear. When alcohol is in your system, the liver prioritizes breaking it down. While that's happening, your body burns less fat for fuel. Research in controlled metabolic settings has shown that drinking alcohol temporarily reduces fat burning, so the fat and carbs you eat around the same time are more likely to be stored rather than used.

Your body turns very little alcohol directly into fat. The bigger effect is indirect: alcohol "cuts in line" for fuel, and everything else you've eaten waits.

### Alcohol calories don't fill you up

Liquid calories in general are less filling than food, and alcohol in particular doesn't seem to trigger the same "I've had enough" signals. People rarely eat less at dinner because they had two glasses of wine first. If anything, the opposite is common.

### Alcohol tends to increase how much you eat

Studies on the so-called aperitif effect have found that drinking alcohol before or with a meal tends to increase how much people eat at that meal. Alcohol also loosens inhibitions, which makes the late-night pizza, fries, or kebab much more appealing than it would be sober.

### The next day costs calories too

A hangover tends to push people toward high-calorie comfort food, sugary drinks, and less movement. Poor sleep after drinking is also linked to stronger cravings the next day. Over a weekend, these indirect effects can easily add more calories than the drinks themselves.

This is why the drink calories on the chart are only part of the picture. A night of four regular beers is about 600 calories in the glass, but the late-night food and the slow, hungry next day can double that.

## Does Alcohol Make You Gain Weight?

It can, but it depends heavily on how much and how often you drink.

The research on moderate drinking and body weight is mixed. Some large observational studies have found that light to moderate drinkers, particularly wine drinkers, don't gain more weight than non-drinkers over time. Others find a clearer link between heavier drinking and weight gain, especially around the waist. These studies can't fully separate alcohol from everything else about drinkers' lifestyles, so they don't prove cause and effect either way.

What's more clearly supported:

- **Heavy and binge drinking** is more consistently linked with weight gain and higher waist circumference than occasional light drinking.
- **The total matters.** Five drinks on a Saturday is roughly 500 to 750 calories before food. Done every weekend, that's a lot of energy across a year.
- **Food choices around drinking** often matter as much as the drinks.

The so-called "beer belly" isn't really caused by beer specifically. It reflects total calories, the tendency of alcohol to shift fat storage, and, for many people, age and genetics that favor storing fat around the middle. Wine and cocktails can do the same thing.

If weight is your concern, our [alcohol and weight loss guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-weight-loss-metabolic-guide-2025) goes deeper into the metabolism and practical strategies.

## Alcohol Calories vs Carbs: Which Matters More?

People on low-carb or keto diets often focus only on carbs. That makes sense for blood sugar, but for total calories, the alcohol is usually the bigger number.

Take a regular 5% beer at around 150 calories: about 98 of those come from alcohol and about 50 from carbs. A "zero-carb" spirit like vodka still has about 97 calories per shot. Choosing straight spirits over beer cuts carbs dramatically, but it doesn't make the drink calorie-free.

There's a second wrinkle for low-carb eaters. While your liver is processing alcohol, it produces less new glucose and burns less fat, which can temporarily slow ketone production. Our [alcohol and keto guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-ketogenic-diet-ketosis-impact-analysis-2025) explains how different drinks affect ketosis.

A safety note: alcohol can lower blood sugar, sometimes hours after you stop drinking, especially if you haven't eaten. This matters most for people who take insulin or certain diabetes medications. If that's you, talk to your doctor, and see our [alcohol and blood sugar guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025).

## Why Calories Aren't on the Label

Most packaged foods in the US must carry a Nutrition Facts panel, but most alcoholic drinks don't. Beer, wine, and spirits are regulated by the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB) rather than the FDA, and calorie labeling is voluntary. Some brands choose to add a "Serving Facts" panel with calories, carbs, and alcohol content, and that's becoming more common, especially for light beers and seltzers. In the European Union, drinks above 1.2% alcohol have also been exempt from the standard nutrition labeling rules, although some producers now share nutrition details voluntarily, sometimes through a QR code.

The practical upshot: if the calories aren't printed, check the brand's website, or use the ABV and serving size with the formula above.

## Simple Ways to Drink Fewer Calories Without Giving Up a Night Out

You don't have to stop drinking to cut a lot of alcohol calories. Small changes add up quickly.

1. **Pick a lower-strength version.** Going from a 7% IPA to a 4% session beer saves around 80 to 100 calories a can. A lower-alcohol wine saves a little per glass.
2. **Watch the pour size.** Measuring wine at 5 ounces instead of 8 saves around 70 to 80 calories a glass.
3. **Use zero-calorie mixers.** Soda water, diet tonic, and sparkling water with fresh lime turn a 180-calorie drink into a 100-calorie one.
4. **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between drinks slows your pace, which usually means fewer drinks overall. It also helps with hydration.
5. **Eat a real meal before drinking.** Food in your stomach slows alcohol absorption and makes the late-night snack run less tempting.
6. **Set a drink count before you start.** Deciding in advance is much easier than deciding three drinks in.
7. **Plan the late-night food.** If you know you'll be hungry, have something reasonable ready at home instead of relying on whatever's open at 1 a.m.
8. **Protect the next day.** Sleep, hydration, and a decent breakfast make it easier to avoid a day of grazing on junk food.

Most of these also help with how you feel the next morning, which brings us to the last piece.

## Calories, Hangovers, and the Morning After

The number of drinks that drives your calorie count is the same number that drives your hangover. Fewer, smaller, lower-strength drinks tend to mean both fewer calories and a gentler next day. Sugary mixed drinks can also make it easier to drink faster than you realize, because the sweetness hides the taste of alcohol.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence. Pacing, eating, and hydration do most of the work.

Some people also add a supplement on nights out. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising but not established. It has no effect on the calories in your drinks, and there is no good evidence that it helps with weight. If you'd like to try it for the morning after, [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a budget-friendly option and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) is a popular all-in-one blend. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## When to Talk to a Doctor

Counting calories is a normal part of managing weight, and for most social drinkers it's a reasonable thing to do. But talk to a doctor or registered dietitian if:

- You have diabetes, take insulin, or take medications that lower blood sugar, since alcohol can cause delayed low blood sugar.
- You have liver disease, pancreatitis, or high triglycerides, where alcohol may need to be limited or avoided.
- You're taking medication that interacts with alcohol.
- You're pregnant or trying to become pregnant.
- You notice you're skipping meals to "save" calories for drinking. Drinking on an empty stomach raises your blood alcohol faster and increases the risk of getting dangerously drunk.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol has about **7 calories per gram**, nearly double carbs or protein.
- Every US standard drink holds about **100 calories from alcohol** before sugar or mixers.
- Typical counts: light beer around 100, regular beer around 150, a 5-ounce glass of wine around 120, a shot of 80-proof liquor around 100, and sweet cocktails anywhere from 250 to over 500.
- **Strength and pour size matter more than the type of drink.**
- Alcohol pauses fat burning while your body clears it, doesn't fill you up, and tends to increase how much you eat, so the real calorie cost of a night out is usually higher than the drinks alone.
- Smaller pours, lower-strength drinks, zero-calorie mixers, and water between rounds cut calories without much sacrifice.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How many calories are in alcohol?**

Pure alcohol has about 7 calories per gram. A US standard drink contains 14 grams of alcohol, so each standard drink carries roughly 100 calories from the alcohol alone. Beer, wine, and mixed drinks add more from carbs and sugar: a regular 12-ounce beer is about 150 calories, a 5-ounce glass of wine about 120, and a 1.5-ounce shot of 80-proof liquor about 97.

**Which alcohol has the fewest calories?**

Straight spirits with a zero-calorie mixer (like vodka and soda water), hard seltzers, light beers, and dry brut sparkling wine are usually the lowest, at around 100 calories per serving. Because calories come mostly from the alcohol, lower-strength drinks in smaller pours will generally be the lightest choice.

**How many calories are in a shot of vodka or tequila?**

A 1.5-ounce shot of 80-proof (40%) vodka, tequila, gin, rum, or whiskey has about 97 calories. At 100 proof it rises to about 124 calories. Unflavored spirits have essentially no carbs, so the calories depend on the proof, not the type of spirit.

**How many calories are in a glass of wine?**

A standard 5-ounce glass of dry wine has about 115 to 130 calories, with reds usually a little higher than whites because they tend to be stronger. Sweet and dessert wines have more. Many home and restaurant pours are 6 to 9 ounces, which can push a single glass to 200 calories or more.

**Do alcohol calories count toward weight gain?**

Yes. Alcohol calories are real energy your body uses. They also pause fat burning while your liver clears the alcohol, don't make you feel full, and often lead to eating more. Heavier and binge drinking are more consistently linked with weight gain than occasional light drinking.

**Why is alcohol called empty calories?**

Because it provides energy with almost no nutritional value. Alcohol doesn't supply vitamins, minerals, protein, or fiber the way food does. The calories still count, they just don't come with anything else your body needs.

**Is beer or liquor worse for calories?**

Per standard drink, they're similar at around 100 calories from alcohol, but beer adds carbs, so a regular beer is about 150 calories versus about 100 for a shot of liquor. Mixed drinks can easily reverse that if they use regular soda, juice, or syrup. Strong craft beers can carry 200 to 350 calories per can.

**Does burning off alcohol calories work like burning off food?**

Not quite. Your body can't store alcohol, so it burns it first, before fat or carbs. While that's happening, the food you've eaten is more likely to be stored. Exercise doesn't speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol, and working out while still drunk or very hungover isn't a good idea.
